extracted.intended_audience: high school newspaper editors and student-staff (editors, advertising/circulation managers, humor editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing the editorial page and managing the business/advertising/circulation functions of a high-school student newspaper, plus diction/style rules for student reporters and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts must support statements
rubrics_metrics.description: All statements must be supported by convincing data. Facts must be the foundation upon which the superstructure of opinion is built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more complete the information and the more logical the presentation of facts, the more forceful and effective the editorial. Do the necessary research to obtain material for a foundation of fact so opinions, conclusions, and suggestions will be truly effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects must be interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Most editorials in the school paper should deal with live topics — topics the students are discussing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some brief philosophical or historical essays are acceptable but should be lively. Avoid long, windy, boresome sermons. Do not moralize or preach; the school editorial should not be fault-finding in tone but should boost school enterprises without nagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step formula for editorial writing: First, state the facts or circumstances; second, state the opinion to be established; third, state the reasons for the opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By following this formula the editorial will be logical and convincing. Variation of order may occur, but every good editorial should contain the material of all three steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone: avoid fault-finding and moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The school editorial should not be fault-finding in tone; it should boost school enterprises without nagging and without preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students generally resist advice from teachers/parents; editorial writers should avoid moralizing harangues or a fault-finding voice that alienates the student readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for the humor column
rubrics_metrics.description: There are just three requisites for humor in the high school paper: originality, kindliness, and decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humor editor should be a friendly person, not a 'smart aleck.' Keep jokes civil, avoid meanness or indecency; examples of acceptable short humorous items are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include varied regular departments
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial page may contain verse, essays, stories, statistical paragraphs, alumni notes, and exchanges under special headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical recurring departments include 'Ventures in Verse,' 'Adventures in the Commonplace,' 'Do You Know That?,' 'Alumni and Former Students,' 'Bits O' News,' and 'What Other Schools Are Doing.' Maintain regular headings and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business staff composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The business staff should include a general business manager, an advertising manager, a circulation manager, several advertising solicitors, and a corps of circulation assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The business manager keeps the books and acts as treasurer; advertising and circulation managers report to him. Heads of editorial staff should consult the business manager before planning special editions or incurring expenses beyond the allotment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business manager fiscal caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The business manager must be exceedingly conservative in handling finances and must hold the editorial staff within a reasonable limit of expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He must know exactly where the money is coming from to meet every bill authorized, keep close checks on advertising and circulation, know the financial condition at all times, and follow a policy to insure the paper's stability and self-support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising solicitor: signed contracts and file copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertising solicitor should procure, if possible, a signed contract for every advertisement he sells and keep all advertising copy on file until published and paid for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many advertisers are careless about paying when authorization is only oral; a signed contract is the only unanswerable protection. Keep the copy received from each advertiser (in a separate envelope) to resolve disputes by comparing published ads with original copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising manager: do not correct advertiser copy without authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: If an advertiser sends in copy with misspelled words or errors, the advertising manager should direct attention to the mistakes but should never correct them without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some advertisers use misspellings deliberately for effect; strict following of copy is necessary. Example: a cleaning/dyeing shop intentionally used 'dying' to attract attention; the paper printed copy as submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising solicitor skill requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertising manager and solicitors should be able, when called upon, to write live advertising copy and to suggest arrangement of material in advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should give sound advice and worthwhile assistance to clients; knowledge of copywriting strengthens solicitation and client service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement: carry the spirit of the store
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertisement should carry the spirit of the store: confidence can be gained by understatement and by the use of man-to-man manner in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frankness, simple language, truthfulness, and clearness. Tone and voice should match the advertiser's identity and inspire trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement: focus on a few points and be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The advertisement should focus on a few points and be specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid listing too many disparate claims; concentrate messaging. Exception: a staples list (e.g., grocery prices) where price is the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement: crowd for a decision (clear call-to-action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The copy should 'crowd for a decision' — state prices, note limited quantities, offer terms of payment, and set a time limit on offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing concrete transactional details increases likelihood of action (sales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement: strive for identity, uniformity, recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account what is coming after this advertisement in the series and strive for identity, uniformity, recognition, cumulative effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a distinctive border, catch phrase, or consistent typographic/graphic element across a series to build recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement objective: attract attention and move to action
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement must have a definite purpose, attract attention, arouse interest, move to action, and remain in the memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy should be original and individual without being freakish or objectionable; it should promote a plan behind the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement set-up essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: The set-up of a good advertisement must include uniform appearance in a series, proper use of white space, contrast, pictures if possible, proper balance, and few simple faces of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictures: line drawings are best for newspaper work; avoid crowding type faces — choose a few simple faces (e.g., Cheltenham or Caslon). Balance means arranging elements for attention, not mere symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of a good advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: A good advertisement is recognized by having a sound merchandising proposition, dominating the page or its part, being easy to read, ringing true with sincerity, and urging to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type should be as easy to read as a primer line ('Mary has a cat'). The copy should feel sincere and backed by a plan for customer response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of a poor advertisement
rubrics_metrics.description: Common poor-ad features include being a mere epitaph (vague label), lacking timeliness or 'brass-tack' facts, running unchanged for several issues, being a space filler, or being perpetually the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ads fail to engage; refresh copy and include timely, concrete information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonest faults in newspaper advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical faults: space crowded with too many words; symmetry sought instead of balance; typefaces fight instead of harmonize; borders fail to make the ad stand out; cuts (illustrations) are lacking or incorrectly used; copy lacks a point of contact and focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overlong copy, conflicting typefaces, and decorative symmetry that dilutes emphasis. Use illustrations appropriately and ensure a clear point of contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation manager: subscription card system
rubrics_metrics.description: Before launching a subscription campaign, print a number of subscription cards equal to the total number of students and teachers; cards should be serially numbered with detachable receipt stubs bearing the same number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each room representative cards equal to their room's enrollment and record serial numbers. Reps must return filled or blank cards; missing stubs/cards make reps financially responsible for one subscription fee. Maintain filing of stubs and signed cards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation manager: recordkeeping and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The circulation manager should solicity subscriptions, keep a list of subscribers, deliver papers, receive all late payments, and file subscriber cards by room alphabetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When distributing, consult files to determine exact number of papers per room representative. This system safeguards against loss/misappropriation of papers and subscription fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational principle for business management
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful organization is of primary importance in every phase of business management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hierarchy, clear responsibilities, contract/file systems, and checks (serial numbers, receipts) are essential to making the paper self-supporting and financially stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'bring forth' for 'produce/offer'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'bring forth' for bring forward, offer, or produce — 'bring forth' means give birth to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: 'He brought forth a tattered book.' Right: 'He produced a tattered book.' Several corrective examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'cause' with predicate noun/clause, not 'on account of/due to'
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause, like reason, should be completed with a predicate noun or noun clause, never by such an expression as 'on account of' or 'due to.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'The cause of my failure was on account of illness.' Right: 'The cause of my failure was illness.' Alternative constructions: 'I failed on account of illness.' 'My failure was due to illness.' 'The cause of my failure was that I was ill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'company' for companion/guest/escort
rubrics_metrics.description: Company should not be used for companion, guest, escort, or the plurals of these words; 'keeping company' is a vulgarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not good: 'We had company last night.' Right: 'We entertained guests last night.' Examples show acceptable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural agreement: data/phenomena/strata
rubrics_metrics.description: Data, phenomena, and strata are plural and take plural verbs; singulars are datum, phenomenon, and stratum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'The data concerning the phenomena of the eclipse is ready.' Right: 'The data concerning the phenomenon of the eclipse are ready.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'date' for appointment or engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Date should not be used for appointment or engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careless: 'The lecturer has a date in New York.' Right: 'The lecturer has an engagement in New York.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'do away with' as weak expression
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do away with' is a weak expression for abolish, discontinue, or eliminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak: 'The new system will do away with waste.' Right: 'The new system will eliminate waste.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction 'don't' ungrammatical with 3rd person singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that 'don't' is a contraction of 'do not' and is ungrammatical when used with a subject in the third person singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'He don't understand the word.' Right: 'He doesn't understand the word.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'fix' for 'repair' or for 'plight/condition'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'fix' to mean 'repair' or substitute 'fix' for 'plight' or 'condition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faulty: 'We shall be in a fix if we can't fix the car.' Better: 'We shall be in a bad situation if we can't repair the car.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'got' and 'proved' to 'gotten' and 'proven'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'got' and 'proved' to 'gotten' and 'proven' — 'gotten' and 'proven' are obsolescent forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not good: 'He has gotten the book and proven the point.' Better: 'He has got his book and proved the point.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse 'guess' with 'think/suppose/expect/intend'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Guess' should not be confused with 'think,' 'suppose,' 'expect,' or 'intend.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not good: 'I guess I'll go, for I guess he is expecting me.' Right: 'I intend to go, for I think he is expecting me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'bunch' for 'group' or 'party'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bunch' should not be used for group or party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'He is one of our bunch.' Right: 'He is one of our party.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'hustle' transitively, not intransitively for 'hasten'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hustle' is a transitive verb and should never be used intransitively for 'hasten.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'We hustled to keep out of the way of the coach.' Right: 'We hurried to keep out of the way of the coach.' Right example of transitive use: 'The coach hustled us up and down the field.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'behind' to 'in back of'; 'in front of' is correct
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In back of' is a crudity for 'behind'; 'in front of' is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'They are playing in back of the house in front of the garage.' Right: 'They are playing behind the house in front of the garage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'kind of'/'sort of' to modify nouns only
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Kind of' and 'sort of' should modify nouns, not verbs, adjectives, or adverbs; do not use the article 'a' with these expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'I sort of wondered what kind of a man you were.' Right: 'I wondered for some reason what sort of man you were.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'line' for 'kind' or 'business'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'line' for 'kind' or 'business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'What line of work do you like? I can give you something in the newspaper line.' Right: 'What kind of work do you like? I can give you something in the newspaper business.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'along the line of' or 'in the line of' for 'about'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'along the line of' or 'in the line of' for 'about' or 'in regard to.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'He talked along the line of reform.' Right: 'He talked on the subject of reform.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mad means insane, not merely angry
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Mad' means insane, not angry; a man may be 'mad with anger' but is not necessarily insane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'John is mad at me.' Right: 'John is angry at (or with) me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'in our midst' — use 'among us'
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of 'in our midst' for 'among us' is forbidden in newspaper offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'There were three notable persons in our midst.' Right: 'There were three notable persons among us.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'nice' correctly (not for 'pleasant' etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep in mind that the true meaning of 'nice' is precise, keen in discrimination, or precisely made; do not use the word for 'pleasant' or 'honorable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'Mary is a nice girl.' Right: 'Mary is an agreeable girl.' Wrong: 'We had a nice time at her house.' Right: 'We had a pleasant time at her home.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper phrasing: avoid 'whipped out' and 'tapped on the shoulder'
rubrics_metrics.description: In newspaper stories guns are never 'whipped out,' and persons arrested are never 'tapped on the shoulder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'Whipping out his gun, the policeman tapped his man on the shoulder.' Right: 'Drawing his revolver, the policeman stepped up to the man and placed him under arrest.' Use precise, professional phrasing.
